title: Inter-request prompt slab pooling and eviction coordinator
creator: Ava Kim
description:
Problem statement:

We observe two correlated sources of inefficiency in our inference runtime on high-concurrency workloads: (1) duplicated prefix KV fragments across concurrent requests that share common prompt prefixes (chat system prompts, system messages, boilerplate templates), and (2) GPU memory fragmentation from variable-sized prefix allocations which reduces effective slab utilization and forces earlier evictions of hot fragments.

Goal:
Design and implement a coordinator that enables inter-request prefix slab pooling and a deterministic eviction policy (Eviction Coordinator) that: (a) coalesces identical or highly-similar prefix fragments across requests, (b) packs deduplicated fragments into compact slabs to improve GPU occupancy, (c) exposes safe eviction hooks to continuous-batching so in-flight KV lookups are consistent, and (d) degrades gracefully under memory pressure with bounded CPU overhead.

Key ideas and approach:
1) Fingerprint + L2 similarity bloom: compute a short (64-bit) stable fingerprint for canonicalized tokenized prefixes and a complementary small sim-hash for fuzzy matches (useful for small prompt template differences). Fingerprint lookup is primary; sim-hash triggers candidate dedupe with a quick token-prefix compare.

2) Slab pooling with variable bucket sizes: allocate fixed-size GPU slabs (e.g., 64MB, 16MB, 4MB) and pack fragments into the smallest slab that can fit them. Maintain per-slab allocation bitmaps and an index to support compaction moves (copy + pointer swap) when fragmentation exceeds threshold.

3) Eviction Coordinator: a central in-process component (single-threaded async actor) per GPU that tracks slab utilization, usage recency via a lightweight access counter, and external signals (batcher backpressure, SLO hints). Eviction happens at slab granularity to minimize pointer churn and enables efficient compaction.

4) Safe pointer swap + epoch barrier for continuous batching: when compaction or dedupe consolidation moves a fragment, we perform an atomic pointer swap and publish a new epoch. In-flight batches that started under prior epoch use a lightweight read-handle referencing the old slab; a grace period (bounded by max request latency + small delta) ensures no use-after-free. Background reclaimer frees slabs after epoch quiescence.

5) Opportunistic dedupe during request admission: during continuous-batching admission, check the canonical fingerprint cache; if found, attach pointer and avoid re-materializing keys. If sim-hash matches but fingerprint differs, prepare a short verification compare (first N tokens) executed asynchronously by a worker thread with priority throttling to avoid blocking hot inference threads.

Trade-offs considered:
- Strong canonicalization (normalize whitespace, template slots) increases dedupe but risks false positives across semantically different prompts. We limit canonicalization to normalization and template slot masking only when the template ID is provided by caller (Console/SDK hint).
- Moving fragments for compaction increases GPU copy bandwidth and transient memory use. We limit compaction frequency and prefer slab-level evictions under high throughput to keep latency stable.
- Single-threaded Eviction Coordinator avoids locks but could be a throughput bottleneck on huge multi-tenant hosts; we'll shard coordinator by GPU and expose a metrics-backed throttling knob.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- M1 (Design + prototyping, 2w): detailed design doc, fingerprint format, sim-hash parameters, slab sizes, epoch protocol. (Owner: Marcus)
- M2 (Runtime primitives, 1w): slab allocator, GPU slab metadata, pointer-table abstraction, epoch publish/subscribe. (Owner: Marcus)
- M3 (Dedupe layer + admission checks, 2w): fingerprint index, sim-hash candidate path, async verifier worker, SDK hints integration. (Owner: Sita Rao)
- M4 (Eviction Coordinator + compaction, 2w): implement coordinator actor, compaction move, grace reclamation. (Owner: Marcus)
- M5 (Integration with continuous-batching, 1w): ensure atomic pointer swap works with batcher, add epoch checks in token lookup path. (Owners: batching team)
- M6 (Canary + perf runs, 1w): deploy to canary fleet, run latency/p50/p95/p99 and memory utilization tests, iterate. (Owners: infra + SRE)

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end correctness: no observed read-after-free under load (verified by stress tests and custom latency + corruption tests).
- Effective dedupe: reduce duplicated prefix memory by >= 30% on chat-template-heavy workloads (internal benchmark).
- GPU occupancy improvement: at least 12% increase in effective occupied memory per GPU under target workload vs baseline (improved packing).
- Batch latency impact: p99 latency increase <= 3% after enabling dedupe/compaction under normal load.
- CPU overhead: additional CPU consumption <= 8% on leader nodes for the coordinator workload.

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: sim-hash false positives cause unnecessary merges and subtle semantic correctness issues. Mitigation: require token-prefix verification before merge completes and keep original fragment until verification passes.
- Risk: epoch grace period miscalculated causing OOM spikes. Mitigation: conservative default grace (latency bound * 2) and fast telemetry to detect long-lived handles; optionally disable compaction for specific noisy workloads.

Telemetry and dashboards:
- New metrics: dedupe_hit_rate, dedupe_candidate_rate, slab_fragmentation_ratio, slab_compactions, coordinator_queue_len, epoch_quiescence_seconds.
- Dashboards: per-GPU slab utilization, memory savings over time, and latency delta pre/post compaction.

- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1246 (WIP)
- Benchmark harness: internal perf repo: https://go.redwood/perf/kv-dedupe-2025
